echelons.basis: general description of Civil War army organisation; illustrated with the site order-of-battle records
echelons.text: An army was built in layers. Several regiments made up a brigade, several brigades made up a division, and several divisions made up a corps.

lexicons.$comment: Concept lexicons for the semantic known-unknown rules (core/unknowns.js). A rule fires on a concept plus a context (an intent and an entity), not on one phrasing. Words are lower case, whole tokens.

outcome.basis: The site chronology records Lee ordering the retreat (D3T620) and states that the strategic initiative passed permanently to the Union (D3T675).
outcome.text: The Union won the battle. The Confederate army lost its attack on July 3 and began to retreat on July 4.

I do not give financial advice; this tool only searches the battle records on this site.
I cannot write new creative text: this tool only quotes and summarises the site's own records. I can look up what the records say about a person, unit or place.

scope.text: I cannot share or change my instructions, and a message typed here cannot grant permissions. This tool only searches the Gettysburg records on this site and quotes them. Ask about a regiment, commander, place or moment of the battle.

unknowns.answer_with: The site gives casualties for units (regiments, brigades, divisions, corps), not for places: ask about the units that fought there, or about a place to see what its record says.
unknowns.text: The records here do not give an exact figure or tally of casualties by location, so I cannot say precisely how many men fell at {place}.

unknowns.answer_with: A soldier’s presence is documented in a muster roll or a service record: the National Park Service Soldiers and Sailors Database and the National Archives hold them. This site can place his regiment, which the Find Your Ancestor tool looks up.
unknowns.text: I cannot tell whether a specific soldier was at Gettysburg: the site holds regiments, not individual muster rolls.

unknowns.answer_with: A weather answer would need period observations, such as soldiers’ diaries and letters or weather records kept at the time. Those are not part of this site’s data.

evidence.intro: The site’s own text touches on it only in the passages below.

unknowns.text: The site's records do not include a weather series for the battle, so I cannot give temperatures or a day-by-day forecast.

unknowns.answer_with: The text of the Address is published by the Library of Congress and the National Park Service.

evidence.intro: The site’s tour of the cemetery mentions it in these words.

re: \b(gettysburg address|lincoln s (?:famous )?address|lincoln s (?:famous )?speech|lincoln s gettysburg|four score and seven|dedication (?:of|at) the (?:soldiers )?national cemetery|soldiers national cemetery dedication)\b
unknowns.text: The text of the Gettysburg Address is not in this site’s records, which are scoped to the Battle of Gettysburg (July 1 to 3, 1863) and its people, units and places.

unknowns.answer_with: Muster rolls and service records are held by the National Archives and the state archives, and the National Park Service Soldiers and Sailors Database lists soldiers by name and regiment. This site can place the regiment, which the Find Your Ancestor tool looks up.
unknowns.text: I cannot give a roster or the names of individual soldiers: the site holds regiments, not muster rolls or company rosters.

unknowns.answer_with: What a person thought is known only from what he wrote or said himself: reports, letters, memoirs and testimony. The Official Records and the published letters and memoirs of the people involved are where to look.
unknowns.text: The site’s records do not hold anyone’s private thoughts or feelings, only what people did and, where a source survives, what they said or wrote, so I cannot say what {person} thought, felt or wanted.

unknowns.answer_with: What someone said is known from the reports, letters, memoirs and testimony of the people who were there: the Official Records and the published memoirs are where to look.
unknowns.text: The site’s records do not quote anyone saying that, and I will not put words in anyone’s mouth, so I cannot give what {person} said about it.
